title: Rolo and the Spooky Shed
markdown:
Rolo and Marmalade loved helping Grandma Bear. Grandma Bear made the most splendid jams in the whole wide forest. Blackberry, raspberry, strawberry. If you could name it, she jarred it. This particular afternoon the air was thick with the sweet scent of warm blackberries. She hummed as she stirred the bubbling jam in her biggest shiniest pot. The last batch of the season. Rolo’s tummy rumbled just thinking about it.

“Almost there, my dears,” she chirped, apron dusted with flour, spectacles perched on the end of her nose. “Just the very last potful to jar up. Oh, but. Oh dearie me.” She frowned, patting her apron pockets, then her little apron drawers. “I seem to be missing the lid for this last most perfect jar of blackberry jam. The very last one.”

Rolo’s bushy tail gave a twitch. He loved Grandma Bear’s jam. He really loved it. And he knew, with a little shiver that went all the way to his furry toes, where the spare lids were kept. In the shed. The shed at the edge of the garden. A bit dark. A bit dusty. And a bit spooky. Dark dusty quiet places made Rolo wobbly-kneed. He was afraid of the unknown, of what his imagination could conjure in shadows.

“Don’t you worry, Grandma Bear,” he said, trying to sound much braver than he felt. He puffed out his chest and made himself look as tall as possible. “Marmalade and I will go and find the lid. We will.” He squeezed Marmalade, who was tucked under his arm. Marmalade’s soft fur was always so comforting.

“We must hurry,” Grandma Bear said cheerfully, though a little worriedly. “This jam will be just perfect, but it needs its lid right away, or it might get too cool.” A cool lid, she implied, was a sad lid indeed. Rolo knew, with a feeling like a tiny grey cloud in his chest, that if he did not go now he might miss the very best jam. If he did not go now, the jam might not be perfect for the picnic tomorrow. He really, really wanted that jam.

“Come on, Marmalade,” he whispered, taking a deep shaky breath. He scooped up his plush friend and tiptoed toward the garden gate. The shed loomed ahead, wooden door slightly ajar, looking like a sleepy yawn in the afternoon sun.

It’s just a door, Rolo told himself, trying to ignore the way his whiskers twitched. A perfectly normal door. Not a yawning mouth. Nope.

He pushed the shed door open. The hinges went louder than he expected, like the shed grumbling hello. Inside it was not pitch black, but sunlight struggled through the dusty windowpanes and cast long wavy shadows. Forgotten flowerpots. A very old rake that looked like a giant metal spider with too many legs. Shadows. Lots of shadows that seemed to dance when he moved.

Rolo’s heart went thump-thump-thumpety-thump. He clutched Marmalade so tightly his plush friend felt like a fuzzy little rock.

“Okay, Marmalade,” he whispered, voice a little squeaky. “We’re looking for a lid. A round shiny lid. It’s for the jam.”

He tried to focus. Then a shadow seemed to stretch and move in the dim light. A giant shadowy creature? His whiskers quivered. He felt a strong urge to turn tail and scamper back to Grandma Bear’s warm kitchen, jam or no jam. He almost froze, paws glued to the dusty floor. Then he felt Marmalade’s soft familiar fur against his cheek. Marmalade, who was always brave with him, who never made him feel silly for being scared.

“Okay, Rolo,” he whispered, a little steadier. “Marmalade is here. We can do this. We just need that lid.”

He shuffled his paws. He squinted over dusty jars and old watering cans. Then he saw it. High up on a shelf, tucked behind a stack of old dented buckets, glinting in a sliver of light: a perfect round jar lid.

“There it is.” A wave of relief. But oh. It was so high. So, so high. Behind a lopsided stack that looked ready to tumble in a breeze. Rolo’s breath hitched. He would have to climb the wobbly buckets. His paws felt slippery. He imagined tumbling down with a loud clatter.

He clutched Marmalade. “You stay right here. I have to go get the lid. Don’t worry. I’ll be right back.”

Leaving his best friend, even for a moment, felt like a heavy stone in his tummy. He stepped onto the lowest bucket. It wobbled. A gust rustled through the shed and the buckets swayed like a boat on a stormy sea. A tremor went up his legs and made his knees feel like jelly. He could almost hear the clang of buckets hitting the floor and feel the dust flying. But he kept climbing, claws finding tiny grips, eyes fixed on the prize. Slowly, carefully, he reached the top. With a triumphant little squeak he grabbed the lid. For a brief terrifying moment the space where Marmalade had been felt cold and empty.

He climbed back down, shaky and proud. He scooped up Marmalade, who gave a little plush purr, and together they scampered into the bright sunshine, the precious lid held carefully in Rolo’s paws. The sunshine felt so good.

Grandma Bear gasped. “My goodness, Rolo. You found it. You are such a brave clever boy.” She took the lid and, with a satisfying pop, sealed the last jar. The kitchen filled with the most wonderful sweet fruity aroma, a smell that promised warmth and happiness.

Rolo watched, heart swelling with a happy buzzy feeling. He looked back toward the shed. He did not give it a lecture. Later, when a particularly shadowy corner of the den made its usual attempt to look like a grumpy badger, Rolo’s whiskers did not droop. His paws did not get clammy. He took a deep breath. The smell of dusty wood filled his nose. He remembered the wobbly buckets, the tremor, the light feeling of reaching the top. He winked at the shadow, knowing it was only a shadow, and went to find a cookie.
